🌎 BEYOND THE 956

Sir Patrick Stewart, the stage-trained actor who became Captain Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films, has died at 86.

Stewart died on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, at his home in Los Angeles, in the care of his wife, Sunny Ozell, following what his family described as a brief journey with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. His death was announced Thursday, October 29, in a statement posted to his official Instagram account and confirmed to The Hollywood Reporter by his representative.

"We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," the statement said. "He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all."

Born July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England, Stewart trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School and joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966, where he remained through 1982, building a reputation as one of Britain's finest classical actors.

That changed in 1987, when he took command of the starship Enterprise as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek: The Next Generation. Over seven seasons and four feature films — Generations, First Contact, Insurrection and Nemesis — Stewart made Picard a captain defined by diplomacy, conviction and moral authority. He returned to the role two decades later as the star of Star Trek: Picard, which ran for three seasons on Paramount+.

On film, Stewart was known around the world as Professor Charles Xavier, the leader of the X-Men, a role he played beginning in 2000 and most recently in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness (2022). His earlier screen roles included Excalibur (1981) and David Lynch's Dune (1984).

The family's statement also remembered his philanthropy and activism on behalf of human rights, survivors of domestic violence, refugees, veterans' mental health services and animal welfare, and said he would be remembered "for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life." In lieu of flowers, the family asked for memorial contributions to the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer's Disease Research Center Fund and the Alzheimer's Foundation of America Caregiver Resources.

Sources: The Hollywood Reporter (via Stewart's representative); official family statement on Stewart's Instagram account; TheWrap.
